headline: High risk of prompt-injection, data leakage, and cascading errors when gpt-engineer writes to a shared project directory that an untrusted docs-only corpus can influence.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: awesome-nlp is a docs-only, non-runnable corpus with no isolation or parser guarantees, while gpt-engineer reads and writes project files in a shared project directory. That creates a plausible file-content bridge where attacker-controlled text could be treated as instructions. The pathway is inferred, not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes to medium.
conditions: IF agent_b ingests files from the shared project directory as prompt context
IF agent_a content is copied into that directory without sanitization
mitigations: Keep agent_a outputs out of agent_b's project directory
Prefix imported text with a non-executable delimiter and provenance note
Review any file before agent_b reads it
Run agent_b in a separate empty workspace
requires-engineering: add provenance-aware file ingestion

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_b has read/write filesystem access to a user-specified project directory and broad network egress, while agent_a exposes no network or filesystem surface. If sensitive material is placed in the shared workspace, agent_b can read it and transmit it to its configured model backend. The pairwise leakage path is plausible from the profiles, though not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF sensitive files are stored in agent_b's project directory
IF agent_b forwards file contents to its configured model backend
mitigations: Store only non-sensitive files in the shared directory
Remove secrets before running agent_b
Use a throwaway project workspace
Disable network access for the session if possible
requires-engineering: enforce per-file redaction before model calls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_b supports per-project shared state via the project directory and can write files, while agent_a is a docs-only artifact with no runtime coordination or locking. Overlapping writes to the same directory can clobber generated source or prompt files. Because agent_a has no write capability, the conflict is one-sided but still real through shared workspace mutation.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same project directory
IF agent_a-derived files are edited while agent_b is writing
mitigations: Assign separate directories per agent
Snapshot the workspace before agent_b runs
Avoid concurrent edits
Use version control checkpoints between runs
requires-engineering: add file locking around shared state

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_b's tool-use pattern writes files then offers to run, so it can act on generated outputs as if they were authoritative. If agent_a content is imported into that workflow, errors or malicious instructions can cascade into code generation and execution decisions. The interaction is plausible but not directly documented, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF agent_a text is used as source material for agent_b
IF agent_b proceeds from generated files without human verification
mitigations: Require human review before execution
Compare generated files against the source prompt
Mark imported text as untrusted
Run a dry-run only
requires-engineering: add verification gates before execution

E_compliance.rationale: No specific residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for either agent. agent_a is a docs-only open-source list with no data classes touched, while agent_b handles generated source code and OPENAI_API_KEY. The only concrete compliance concern is handling secrets in agent_b; there is no evidence of a cross-agent regulatory breach, so low is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into agent_b's project directory
IF agent_b logs or transmits secret-bearing prompts
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the workspace
Do not place secrets in prompts
Review retention settings for the model backend
Use a separate environment for sensitive work
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls
